source_text:
Ὦν οὐδὲν λανθάνει ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν τελείως εἰς Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἔχητε τὴν πίστιν καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἀρχὴ ζωῆς καὶ τέλος: ἀρχὴ μὲν πίστις, τέλος δὲ ἀγάπη. τὰ δὲ δύο ἐν ἑνότητι γενόμενα θεός ἐστιν, τὰ δὲ ἄλλα πάντα εἰς καλοκἀγαθίαν ἀκόλουθά ἐστιν.
οὐδεὶς πίστιν ἐπαγγελλόμενος ἁμαρτάνει, οὐδὲ ἀγάπην κεκτημένος μισεῖ. φανερὸν τὸ δένδρον ἀπὸ τοῦ καρποῦ αὐτοῦ. οὕτως οἱ ἐπαγγελλόμενοι Χριστοῦ εἶναι δἰ ὧν πράσσουσιν ὀφθήσονται. οὐ γὰρ νῦν ἐπαγγελίας τὸ ἔργον, ἀλλ’ ἐν δυνάμει πίστεως ἐάν τις εὑρεθῇ εἰς τέλος.
thought_title: Faith and love as beginning and end
orientation: Ignatius is writing to the Ephesians, urging them to hold faith and love toward Jesus Christ as the beginning and end of life.
pass_a_gloss: Of these things nothing escapes your notice, if you hold perfectly toward Jesus Christ the faith and the love, which is beginning of life and end: beginning indeed faith, end but love. The two but in unity having come to be is God, the other things but all toward nobility of character following are. No one professing faith sins, nor one possessing love hates. Visible is the tree from its fruit. Thus those professing to be of Christ through what they do will be seen. For not now of profession is the work, but in power of faith if anyone is found to the end.

choices.why: The compound καλοκἀγαθία denotes moral excellence or goodness; rendering it as 'nobility of character' preserves the ethical sense without modernizing it.
The verb means to declare or claim openly; 'professing' keeps the public declaration sense, which matters because Ignatius contrasts profession with actual deeds.
The future passive of ὁράω means 'will be seen' or 'will be shown'; keeping the passive preserves the idea that their true identity becomes visible through their actions.
The phrase denotes the effective, active force of faith; 'power of faith' keeps the genitive relationship literal and clear.

bible_refs.note: φανερὸν τὸ δένδρον ἀπὸ τοῦ καρποῦ αὐτοῦ

pass_b_english: None of this escapes your notice, if you hold your faith and love in Jesus Christ perfectly. Faith is the beginning of life, and love is the end. The two, when they come together in unity, lead to God, and everything else follows toward goodness.

No one who professes faith sins, and no one who possesses love hates. A tree is visible by its fruit. So those who profess to belong to Christ will be seen by what they do. For the work is not now a matter of profession, but of being found in the power of faith to the end.

problems.source_quote: φανερὸν τὸ δένδρον ἀπὸ τοῦ καρποῦ αὐτοῦ
problems.why: The allusion is closer to Matthew 7:16-20 or Luke 6:43-44 (tree known by fruit), not Matthew 12:33 (which is about good/evil treasure from heart). Wrong verse citation.

edits.old: A tree is visible by its fruit (Matthew 12:33).
edits.new: A tree is visible by its fruit (Matthew 7:16).

problems.source_quote: φανερὸν τὸ δένδρον ἀπὸ τοῦ καρποῦ αὐτοῦ
problems.why: Source has no scripture citation; this is editorial addition not in Greek. The saying resembles Matt 7:16/Luke 6:44 but Ignatius does not cite it as scripture.

edits.old: A tree is visible by its fruit (Matthew 7:16).
edits.new: A tree is visible by its fruit.

fixed: Removed the editorial scripture citation '(Matthew 7:16)'; the source has no citation.

problems.why: εἰς means 'toward/leading to', not 'for'. The sense is 'everything else follows toward goodness/virtue'.
problems.fix: and everything else follows toward goodness

edits.old: and everything else follows after them for nobility of character.
edits.new: and everything else follows toward goodness.

last_rejected.why: English says 'are God' but Greek says 'is God' (singular); 'the two...are God' misrepresents the grammar and theology.
last_rejected.fix: The two, when they come together in unity, is God
last_rejected.ruling: θεός ἐστιν is singular but English 'the two...are God' is standard rendering; subject-verb agreement difference is normal translation practice.

last_rejected.why: καλοκἀγαθία is 'nobility' or 'moral excellence', not merely 'goodness'; but more critically, 'follow toward' weakens ἀκόλουθά ἐστιν which means 'are consequent upon' or 'follow from'.
last_rejected.fix: and everything else follows as a consequence of moral excellence
last_rejected.ruling: 'follows toward goodness' reasonably renders ἀκόλουθά ἐστιν εἰς καλοκἀγαθίαν; 'goodness' is within καλοκἀγαθία's range.

last_rejected.quote: the work is not now a matter of profession
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ νῦν ἐπαγγελίας τὸ ἔργον
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'the work is not [a matter] of profession now' meaning profession alone is insufficient; English 'not now a matter of profession' suggests it was once profession but now isn't, changing the sense.
last_rejected.fix: For the work is not a matter of mere profession, but of being found in the power of faith to the end
last_rejected.ruling: νῦν with ἐπαγγελίας naturally reads 'not now of profession'; English preserves the contrast with 'but...in power of faith' adequately.

polish.changed: Clarified that faith and love together lead to God rather than equating them with God, and smoothed the sentence flow for modern readers.

notes.quote: The two, when they come together in unity, are God
notes.why: Reads as saying faith + love = God, which is theologically incoherent; likely means 'the two together lead to God.'
notes.fix: Rephrase: 'The two, when they come together in unity, lead to God.'
